title: What Were Human Zoos?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore human zoos, the 19th and early 20th century practice of displaying living people from colonized regions in exhibits at fairs, zoos and villages in Europe and the United States. They cover the progression from curiosity and anthropology to public exhibitions, the Paris Colonial Exposition, Belgium's Congo exhibits including King Leopold II and the 1958 Brussels World's Fair, and the 1904 St. Louis World's Fair with the Igorot village and dog-eating ritual. A major focus is Ota Benga, a Mbuti man taken by Samuel Verner to the 1904 fair and then displayed at the Bronx Zoo, his release secured by Black Baptist ministers including Reverend James Gordon, and his later suicide. They also discuss Saartjie Baartman, modern human safaris in the Andaman Islands, a 2014-era Oslo protest art recreation, and close with a listener mail segment about adopting an elephant through the David Sheldrick Wildlife Trust.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to human zoos
segments.summary: Hosts open with off-topic banter about miso soup, then introduce human zoos as a dark chapter, comparing them to Epcot's country pavilions as the wrong way to present other cultures.

segments.title: Origins: curiosity, anthropology and the hierarchy of races
segments.summary: Explanation of how early European encounters with people from other regions turned into study and display, including the rise of biological anthropology in the early 1800s with its racial hierarchy, and the transition to public exhibitions.

segments.title: Peak of colonialism and the Paris Colonial Exposition
segments.summary: Hosts describe the peak of colonialism as the point when the public was brought in, comparing the propaganda to Roman writing about the Druids, and describe the Paris Colonial Exposition recreating indigenous villages. Performers faced poor living conditions, disease, and unmarked mass graves.

segments.title: Belgian Congo exhibits and King Leopold II
segments.summary: Discussion of Belgian displays of Congolese people, including Congorama, King Leopold II bringing 267 Congolese to Brussels, Belgium's control of the Congo after the Berlin conference, and the 1958 World's Fair village where people were paid but many died.

segments.title: Film, the end of human zoos and Mondo Cane
segments.summary: Hosts discuss how human zoos declined after the mid-twentieth century and how films such as Mondo Cane carried the same exoticizing approach onto screen.

segments.title: Ota Benga's life and display at the Bronx Zoo
segments.summary: Biography of Ota Benga: family killed by the Force Publique during rubber quotas, enslavement, display at the 1904 St. Louis World's Fair brought by Samuel Verner, then exhibition in the Bronx Zoo with apes. Black ministers protested and secured his release to Reverend James Gordon, who tried to help him integrate. He later died by suicide in Virginia after failing to return to Africa because of World War One.

segments.title: 1904 St. Louis World's Fair, Igorot village and Saartjie Baartman
segments.summary: Hosts describe the Igorot village at the St. Louis fair, the Filipino Igorot people, the reported daily dog sacrifice and their display of rituals, and the crowds who paid to attend. They then discuss Saartjie Baartman, displayed in London and Paris, whose remains were repatriated to South Africa in 2002.

segments.title: Modern human safaris, Oslo protest art and the 1958 photo
segments.summary: Discussion of modern human safaris to the Jarawa tribe on the Andaman Islands, the legacy of human zoos in present-day racism, a protest art recreation in Oslo, and the 1958 Brussels photo of a Congolese girl.
